papers.title: Introduction to History: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on introduction to history, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a primary source of history?
questions.explanation:
Primary sources date from the time being studied, such as letters, diaries, artefacts and eyewitness accounts. Later accounts are secondary sources.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a textbook written by a modern historian: A textbook written later is a secondary source.
- a film made today about the slave trade: A modern film is a later interpretation, a secondary source.
- a newspaper article reviewing a history book: A review of a history book is a secondary source.

options.label: A
options.content: a letter written by a trader in the year described

options.label: B
options.content: a textbook written by a modern historian

options.label: C
options.content: a film made today about the slave trade

options.label: D
options.content: a newspaper article reviewing a history book

questions.stem: Which source is most important for reconstructing the history of West African societies that did not use writing?
questions.explanation:
Oral tradition, passed down by elders, griots and court historians, preserves the history of societies without writing, and is cross-checked with archaeology and other sources.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- government gazettes: Gazettes are written records produced by colonial and modern governments.
- census reports: Censuses are modern written records.
- printed newspapers: Newspapers arrived with Western printing in the nineteenth century.

questions.stem: The study of past human societies by excavating and examining material remains is called
questions.explanation:
Archaeology studies the past through material remains such as tools, pottery, buildings and bones, recovered by excavation.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- anthropology: Anthropology studies human societies and cultures, mostly living ones.
- linguistics: Linguistics studies languages and their relationships.
- numismatics: Numismatics is the study of coins only.

questions.stem: In which century did the year 1482 fall?
questions.explanation:
The century is one more than the hundreds figure: 1482 has 14 hundreds, so it is in the 15th century (1401–1500).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the fourteenth century: The fourteenth century covers 1301–1400.
- the sixteenth century: The sixteenth century covers 1501–1600.
- the thirteenth century: The thirteenth century covers 1201–1300.

questions.stem: A major weakness of oral tradition as a historical source is that it
questions.explanation:
Oral traditions can be altered, shortened or exaggerated over generations, may favour ruling families, and are hard to date, so historians cross-check them with other sources.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- cannot be used for African history: Oral tradition is a vital source for African history.
- is always written in Arabic: Oral tradition is spoken, not written.
- records only European activities: Oral tradition records the history of local peoples.

options.label: A
options.content: cannot be used for African history

options.label: D
options.content: may change or be exaggerated as it is passed down

papers.topic: The Land and Peoples of West Africa
papers.title: The Land and Peoples of West Africa: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on the land and peoples of west africa, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Why did the large empires of Ghana, Mali and Songhai develop in the savanna rather than the forest?
questions.explanation:
Open savanna country allowed horses and cavalry, easy movement of armies and traders, and contact with trans-Saharan trade, so large empires grew there.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the savanna had the most rainfall in West Africa: The forest, not the savanna, has the most rainfall.
- the savanna was closest to the Atlantic coast: The savanna empires were far from the coast, on the Sahara's edge.
- the tsetse fly was common in the savanna: The tsetse fly was a problem mainly in the forest, limiting horses there.

options.label: A
options.content: open grassland allowed horses, cavalry and easy movement for trade

options.label: B
options.content: the savanna had the most rainfall in West Africa

options.label: C
options.content: the savanna was closest to the Atlantic coast

options.label: D
options.content: the tsetse fly was common in the savanna

questions.stem: Which insect limited the use of horses in the forest zone of West Africa?
questions.explanation:
The tsetse fly spreads trypanosomiasis, which kills horses and cattle, so forest states relied more on infantry than cavalry.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the locust: Locusts destroy crops but did not stop the use of horses.
- the mosquito: Mosquitoes spread malaria among people, not the horse disease that limited cavalry.
- the termite: Termites damage wood and buildings, not horses.

questions.stem: The Hausa and Kanuri languages belong to which language families respectively?
questions.explanation:
Hausa is a Chadic language in the Afro-Asiatic family; Kanuri belongs to the Nilo-Saharan family. Most other West African languages are Niger-Congo.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Niger-Congo and Afro-Asiatic: Hausa is Afro-Asiatic, but Kanuri is Nilo-Saharan, not Afro-Asiatic.
- Nilo-Saharan and Niger-Congo: This reverses Hausa's family; Hausa is Afro-Asiatic (Chadic).
- Niger-Congo and Niger-Congo: Neither Hausa nor Kanuri is a Niger-Congo language.

questions.stem: A society governed by elders, age grades and village councils without a king is described as
questions.explanation:
Decentralised (acephalous) societies, such as many Igbo communities, were governed by elders, age grades, title societies and village assemblies, without a single ruler.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- centralised: A centralised society has a king or chief with a central government.
- theocratic: A theocracy is ruled by religious leaders according to religious law.
- feudal: Feudalism was a European system of lords and vassals based on land.

questions.stem: Which two ethnic groups are the largest in Sierra Leone?
questions.explanation:
The Temne and Mende each make up roughly a third of Sierra Leone's population; the country has about sixteen ethnic groups.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the Krio and the Limba: The Krio and Limba are important but smaller groups.
- the Fula and the Mandinka: Fula and Mandinka communities are smaller, mainly in the north.
- the Kono and the Sherbro: The Kono and Sherbro are much smaller than the Temne and Mende.

papers.title: Early West African States: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on early west african states, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Ancient Ghana was founded by the
questions.explanation:
Ancient Ghana, called Wagadu by its people, was founded by the Soninke in the area of present-day Mauritania and Mali.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Mandinka: The Mandinka founded Mali under Sundiata.
- Songhai: The Songhai founded the Songhai empire based at Gao.
- Hausa: The Hausa built city-states such as Kano and Katsina further east.

questions.stem: The Mali empire was founded by Sundiata Keita after his victory at the battle of
questions.explanation:
Sundiata defeated Sumanguru of Sosso at Kirina in about 1235 and founded the Mali empire.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Tondibi: Tondibi (1591) was the Moroccan victory that ended Songhai.
- Feyiase: Feyiase (1701) was Asante's victory over Denkyira.
- Tabkin Kwotto: Tabkin Kwotto (1804) was an early victory of Usman dan Fodio's jihad.

questions.stem: Mansa Musa of Mali is best remembered for
questions.explanation:
Mansa Musa's hajj of 1324, with great quantities of gold, made Mali famous across North Africa and Europe; he also built mosques and encouraged scholarship.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- founding the city of Gao: Gao was an old Songhai centre, not founded by Mansa Musa.
- defeating the Moroccan army at Tondibi: The Moroccans won at Tondibi in 1591, long after Musa.
- introducing Christianity into Mali: Mansa Musa was a devout Muslim who spread Islam.

options.label: B
options.content: defeating the Moroccan army at Tondibi

questions.stem: Which ruler reformed the government of Songhai, divided it into provinces and made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1496–1497?
questions.explanation:
Askia Muhammad (1493–1528) reorganised Songhai into provinces, created a professional army, standardised weights and measures, promoted Islam and made the hajj.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Sunni Ali: Sunni Ali built the empire by conquest but was not a reformer of this kind.
- Sundiata Keita: Sundiata founded Mali, not Songhai.
- Mansa Musa: Mansa Musa ruled Mali and made his pilgrimage in 1324.

questions.stem: The Songhai empire collapsed after the invasion of
questions.explanation:
A Moroccan army with firearms defeated Songhai at Tondibi in 1591, after which the empire broke up.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the Almoravids in 1076: The Almoravids attacked Ancient Ghana in 1076.
- the Portuguese in 1482: The Portuguese built Elmina on the coast in 1482 and never invaded Songhai.
- the Fulani jihadists in 1804: The Fulani jihad began in Hausaland in 1804, long after Songhai fell.

papers.topic: Trans-Saharan Trade and the Spread of Islam
papers.title: Trans-Saharan Trade and the Spread of Islam: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on trans-saharan trade and the spread of islam, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which animal made the trans-Saharan trade possible on a large scale?
questions.explanation:
The camel can travel long distances with little water, so camel caravans made regular crossings of the Sahara possible.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the horse: Horses need much water and could not cross the Sahara reliably.
- the donkey: Donkeys were used locally but could not make long desert crossings.
- the ox: Oxen cannot survive long without water and grazing.

questions.stem: The main commodities exchanged in the trans-Saharan trade were
questions.explanation:
West Africa exported gold, kola, ivory and slaves northwards, and imported salt, horses, cloth and books from the north.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- salt from the south and gold from the north: This reverses the trade: gold came from West Africa and salt from the Sahara.
- guns from the south and kola from the north: Kola went north from the forest; guns came mainly later from Europeans by sea.
- rubber from the south and cocoa from the north: Rubber and cocoa were colonial-era exports, not trans-Saharan goods.

options.label: A
options.content: salt from the south and gold from the north

options.label: B
options.content: guns from the south and kola from the north

options.label: C
options.content: rubber from the south and cocoa from the north

options.label: D
options.content: gold from the south and salt from the north

questions.stem: Which town was the most famous centre of Islamic learning in the Western Sudan?
questions.explanation:
Timbuktu, with the Sankore mosque and many scholars and libraries, was the leading centre of Islamic learning in Mali and Songhai.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Elmina: Elmina was a Portuguese castle on the Gold Coast.
- Kumasi: Kumasi was the capital of Asante in the forest.
- Ouidah: Ouidah was a slave-trading port of Dahomey on the coast.

questions.stem: One major reason why West African rulers accepted Islam was that it
questions.explanation:
Islam brought Arabic literacy, so rulers gained scribes and officials, as well as trade links, law and prestige in the Muslim world.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- required them to abandon all trade with North Africa: Islam strengthened trade links with North Africa.
- was brought by Portuguese missionaries: Islam came across the Sahara with Muslim traders and clerics.
- forbade the use of written records: Islam brought Arabic literacy and written records.

options.label: A
options.content: required them to abandon all trade with North Africa

options.label: B
options.content: provided literate officials who could keep records and write letters

options.label: D
options.content: forbade the use of written records

questions.stem: Islam reached Sierra Leone mainly through
questions.explanation:
Fula and Mandinka (and Susu) traders and Muslim clerics, many linked to Futa Jallon, brought Islam into northern Sierra Leone.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Portuguese sailors on the coast: The Portuguese were Christians; they did not spread Islam.
- British colonial officials: British officials did not spread Islam.
- the Nova Scotian settlers: The Nova Scotians were mostly Christians.

options.label: C
options.content: Fula and Mandinka traders and clerics from the north

papers.topic: The Forest States of West Africa
papers.title: The Forest States of West Africa: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on the forest states of west africa, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In the Oyo empire, the council that could ask the Alaafin to commit suicide was the
questions.explanation:
The Oyo Mesi, a council of seven nobles led by the Bashorun, could reject a bad Alaafin by presenting an empty calabash or parrot's eggs, meaning he must take his own life.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Ogboni: The Ogboni was a society that checked the Oyo Mesi and represented the earth cult.
- Are-Ona-Kakanfo: The Are-Ona-Kakanfo was the head of the army.
- Asantehene's council: The Asantehene ruled Asante, not Oyo.

questions.stem: The Golden Stool of Asante is associated with
questions.explanation:
Tradition says the priest Okomfo Anokye brought the Golden Stool down from the sky for Osei Tutu; it became the symbol of Asante unity.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Agaja and Gezo: Agaja and Gezo were kings of Dahomey.
- Ewuare and Esigie: Ewuare and Esigie were Obas of Benin.
- Oranmiyan and Afonja: Oranmiyan was linked to the founding of Oyo; Afonja revolted at Ilorin.

questions.stem: Asante gained its independence from Denkyira after the battle of
questions.explanation:
Osei Tutu's Asante defeated Denkyira at Feyiase in 1701, freeing Asante and making it the leading Akan power.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Kirina in 1235: Kirina was Sundiata's victory that founded Mali.
- Tondibi in 1591: Tondibi was the Moroccan victory over Songhai.
- Abomey in 1892: Abomey was Dahomey's capital, taken by the French in 1892.

questions.stem: The kingdom of Dahomey was famous for its
questions.explanation:
Dahomey's centralised state at Abomey had a famous army that included women soldiers, called Amazons by Europeans.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- council of forty scholars: A council of forty scholars governed Masina, not Dahomey.
- Golden Stool: The Golden Stool belongs to Asante.
- cavalry of the Oyo Mesi: The Oyo Mesi was a council of Oyo, not Dahomey's army.

questions.stem: Benin City was captured and its famous bronzes looted by the British in
questions.explanation:
After a British party was killed in January 1897, a punitive expedition captured Benin City in February 1897, looted the Benin Bronzes and exiled Oba Ovonramwen.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1807: 1807 was the year Britain abolished the slave trade.
- 1861: 1861 was the year Britain annexed Lagos.
- 1914: 1914 was the year Nigeria was amalgamated.

papers.topic: The Coming of Europeans to West Africa
papers.title: The Coming of Europeans to West Africa: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on the coming of europeans to west africa, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which European nation was the first to explore the West African coast in the fifteenth century?
questions.explanation:
Portugal, encouraged by Prince Henry the Navigator, led the exploration of the West African coast from the early fifteenth century.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Britain: The English arrived on the coast later, in the sixteenth century.
- France: French traders came after the Portuguese.
- the Netherlands: The Dutch arrived in the late sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

questions.stem: Which of the following was a motive for Portuguese exploration of West Africa?
questions.explanation:
The Portuguese sought gold, a sea route to India and its spices, Christian allies such as Prester John, and to outflank Muslim traders.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- to escape the Industrial Revolution: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the eighteenth century.
- to enforce the abolition of the slave trade: Abolition came in the nineteenth century.
- to obey the Berlin Conference: The Berlin Conference was held in 1884–85.

options.label: A
options.content: to find a sea route to India

options.label: C
options.content: to enforce the abolition of the slave trade

questions.stem: Elmina Castle, the first European fort in West Africa, was built by the Portuguese in
questions.explanation:
The Portuguese built São Jorge da Mina (Elmina) on the Gold Coast in 1482 to protect their gold trade.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1462: 1462 was when Pedro de Sintra named Sierra Leone.
- 1562: 1562 was the year of John Hawkins's first slaving voyage.
- 1652: 1652 is too late; Elmina was built in the fifteenth century.

questions.stem: Which crop was introduced into West Africa from the Americas through European contact?
questions.explanation:
Maize, cassava, groundnuts, sweet potatoes and tomatoes came from the Americas and became staple foods in West Africa.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- yam: Yams are native to West Africa.
- African rice: African rice was domesticated in West Africa long before European contact.
- kola: Kola is a West African forest tree.

questions.stem: Early European traders on the West African coast generally
questions.explanation:
Until the late nineteenth century, Europeans stayed mainly on the coast, paying rent and customs to African rulers who kept control of the interior.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- ruled the interior directly as colonies: European rule of the interior came only in the late nineteenth century.
- refused to trade with African middlemen: Europeans depended on African middlemen for trade.
- built railways to the interior: Railways came in the colonial period.

options.label: A
options.content: ruled the interior directly as colonies

options.label: B
options.content: refused to trade with African middlemen

options.label: C
options.content: paid rent to African rulers for the land on which their forts stood

papers.title: The Atlantic Slave Trade: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on the atlantic slave trade, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The main cause of the Atlantic slave trade was
questions.explanation:
European plantations of sugar, tobacco, cotton and coffee, and mines in the Americas, needed huge amounts of labour after the Native American population collapsed.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the need for soldiers in European wars: Enslaved Africans were taken mainly as plantation and mine labour.
- the spread of Islam in West Africa: Islam's spread was not the cause of the Atlantic trade.
- the shortage of land in Africa: The trade was driven by demand in the Americas, not land shortage in Africa.

options.label: A
options.content: the need for soldiers in European wars

options.label: B
options.content: the spread of Islam in West Africa

options.label: C
options.content: the shortage of land in Africa

options.label: D
options.content: the demand for labour on plantations and in mines in the Americas

questions.stem: The Middle Passage was the
questions.explanation:
In the triangular trade, the Middle Passage was the second leg, carrying enslaved Africans from West Africa across the Atlantic in terrible conditions.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- route of goods from Europe to West Africa: That was the first leg of the triangular trade.
- route of sugar and cotton from the Americas to Europe: That was the third leg of the triangular trade.
- caravan route across the Sahara: That was the trans-Saharan trade, not the Atlantic trade.

options.label: A
options.content: voyage of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to the Americas

options.label: B
options.content: route of goods from Europe to West Africa

options.label: C
options.content: route of sugar and cotton from the Americas to Europe

questions.stem: Which goods did European traders mainly bring to West Africa in exchange for captives?
questions.explanation:
European ships brought manufactured goods such as guns, gunpowder, cloth, iron bars, beads and alcohol to exchange for captives.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- sugar, tobacco, cotton and rum: These plantation goods went from the Americas to Europe.
- gold, ivory, kola and pepper: These were West African exports, not European imports.
- salt, horses and books from North Africa: These came across the Sahara in the trans-Saharan trade.

options.label: B
options.content: guns, cloth, iron bars, beads and alcohol

options.label: D
options.content: salt, horses and books from North Africa

questions.stem: Which of the following was an effect of the Atlantic slave trade on West Africa?
questions.explanation:
The trade took millions of young people, caused depopulation, wars and insecurity, spread firearms, and harmed farming and crafts.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- rapid growth of local industries: Imported goods and insecurity harmed local crafts.
- the end of warfare between states: The trade fuelled wars and raids for captives.
- the spread of the camel across the forest: Camels were used in the Sahara, not the forest.

options.label: B
options.content: the end of warfare between states

options.label: C
options.content: loss of millions of young and productive people

options.label: D
options.content: the spread of the camel across the forest

questions.stem: Bunce Island in the Sierra Leone River was
questions.explanation:
Bunce Island was one of the most important British slave-trading forts on the Upper Guinea coast, shipping many captives to South Carolina and Georgia.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the first settlement of the Nova Scotians: The Nova Scotians founded Freetown in 1792.
- a Portuguese mission school: Bunce Island was a British trading fort.
- the capital of the Sierra Leone Protectorate: The Protectorate was governed from Freetown.

options.label: A
options.content: the first settlement of the Nova Scotians

options.label: C
options.content: the capital of the Sierra Leone Protectorate

papers.topic: Abolition of the Slave Trade and Its Consequences
papers.title: Abolition of the Slave Trade and Its Consequences: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on abolition of the slave trade and its consequences, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In which year did Britain pass the Act abolishing the slave trade?
questions.explanation:
The Abolition of the Slave Trade Act of 1807 made it illegal for British subjects to take part in the slave trade.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1787: In 1787 the abolition society was formed and the Province of Freedom founded.
- 1833: The 1833 Act abolished slavery itself in most British colonies.
- 1865: Slavery was abolished in the United States in 1865.

questions.stem: Which of these men was a leading British abolitionist?
questions.explanation:
William Wilberforce led the campaign in Parliament, with Granville Sharp, Thomas Clarkson and others, to abolish the slave trade.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- John Hawkins: John Hawkins was an English slave trader of the sixteenth century.
- Frederick Lugard: Lugard was a colonial administrator in Nigeria.
- Pedro de Sintra: Pedro de Sintra was a Portuguese explorer who named Sierra Leone.

questions.stem: Freetown was important in enforcing abolition because it was
questions.explanation:
The West Africa Squadron was based at Freetown from 1808; captured slave ships were tried there and freed Africans were landed and settled there.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the headquarters of the slave trade on the coast: Freetown was founded for freed Africans and opposed the trade.
- the capital of French West Africa: French West Africa was governed from Dakar.
- the main port of the Atlantic slave trade to Brazil: Freetown was the centre of anti-slavery work.

options.label: A
options.content: the headquarters of the slave trade on the coast

options.label: B
options.content: the base of the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron

options.label: C
options.content: the capital of French West Africa

options.label: D
options.content: the main port of the Atlantic slave trade to Brazil

questions.stem: Legitimate trade refers to trade in
questions.explanation:
After abolition, Europeans encouraged trade in agricultural and forest produce, especially palm oil, palm kernels, groundnuts and timber.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- slaves carried under licence from the Crown: Legitimate trade replaced the slave trade.
- gold and salt across the Sahara: That was the older trans-Saharan trade.
- guns sold only to African rulers: Legitimate trade means produce, not arms.

options.label: A
options.content: slaves carried under licence from the Crown

options.label: B
options.content: gold and salt across the Sahara

options.label: C
options.content: palm oil, groundnuts and other produce instead of slaves

options.label: D
options.content: guns sold only to African rulers

questions.stem: Which of the following was a consequence of the abolition of the slave trade in West Africa?
questions.explanation:
Abolition led to legitimate trade, freed settlements in Sierra Leone and Liberia, missions and Western education, new educated elites, and greater European involvement inland.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the immediate end of domestic slavery everywhere: Domestic slavery continued in many places for decades.
- the revival of the Songhai empire: Songhai had fallen in 1591.
- the withdrawal of all Europeans from the coast: European involvement in fact grew after abolition.

options.label: A
options.content: the immediate end of domestic slavery everywhere

options.label: B
options.content: the revival of the Songhai empire

options.label: C
options.content: the withdrawal of all Europeans from the coast

options.label: D
options.content: the spread of Christian missions and Western education
